name: Mechanical traction table

lead: A mechanical traction table is a motorised table that applies a controlled pulling force to the spine, often marketed as non-surgical spinal decompression (the DRX9000 is a well-known brand). In height-focused communities it is discussed as a way to decompress the discs and make the most of the spine's full length.

Clinical studies of such devices look at back pain and disc height rather than adult stature. One retrospective cohort reported that restored disc height after a course of motorised decompression went along with less discogenic low back pain [1]. Measured height also naturally varies by roughly a centimetre or more across a day [3].

paras: Sessions are typically delivered in a physiotherapy or chiropractic clinic over a series of weeks, with the person lying on the table in a harness while the device cycles pulling force. Some people in height communities pair traction or inversion with posture and core work.

Clinic traction is generally used for back and neck conditions. In surgical settings, traction tables have been linked to perineal skin injury, nerve palsies and compartment syndrome in the well leg [2][4]. People with spinal instability, fractures or osteoporosis are usually screened by clinicians before traction.

chain: Spine sits at fuller length with better posture
angle.text: People use traction to decompress the spine so that discs sit at their fullest height and posture is more upright. Any change shows up as a small difference in measured or apparent standing height, not a change in bone length.

lead: A mechanical traction table is a motorised table that applies a controlled longitudinal pulling force to the spine, usually through harnesses at the pelvis and chest. Clinics market this as non-surgical spinal decompression, and the DRX9000 is one widely known device of the type [1]. Orthopaedic operating rooms also use a different device called a traction table to hold a leg in position during hip and femur surgery [2].

In looksmaxxing and height communities the interest is in the spine itself. Discs lose a little height under load across the day, and people who want every millimetre of standing height see decompression as a way to recover that height and to support better posture, which can make someone look taller and more upright [3].

Published research on clinical traction centres on pain and disc height rather than stature in adults. Reviews report short-term pain relief from mechanical traction in some radiculopathy patients, with mixed longer-term results [4][5].
infobox: Low back and neck pain, radiculopathy
Spinal decompression for height and posture

paras: A mechanical traction table has a split table, a pelvic harness and a thoracic harness, with a motor that varies the pulling force over a session. The pull can be continuous or intermittent. Spinal traction is described in physical therapy for cervical and lumbar disorders such as radiculopathy and stenosis [4].
Non-surgical spinal decompression is a term used for traction-based care and is distinct from surgical decompression of the spine [5].

The same phrase refers to orthopaedic operating tables that hold a limb under traction for fracture fixation, hip arthroscopy and some hip replacements [2]. A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials compared hip replacement through the direct anterior approach with and without a traction table, finding about 102 mL more blood loss with the table [6]. These devices are not used for height.

Height-focused users describe decompression as a way to counter daily disc compression and to support posture, usually alongside hanging, inversion or stretching. Human height normally varies over the day; one study of 100 children averaged about 1.5 cm lower in the late afternoon than the morning [3]. Proponents therefore see a rested, decompressed spine as the basis for measuring and presenting at full height.

A retrospective cohort study of a six-week course of motorised non-surgical decompression reported that restoration of disc height was associated with decreased discogenic low back pain [1]. A registered trial (NCT04507074) examined traction forces in people with obesity and chronic low back pain [7].

A 2022 meta-analysis summarised in an encyclopedia entry found mechanical traction relieved short-term pain in radiculopathy with the patient supine, while guidelines for cervical traction rest on lower-quality evidence [4]. No published trial has measured permanent change in adult standing height from traction tables.

In surgery, traction tables have documented complications including injury to the perineal skin and soft tissue, neurological impairment and compartment syndrome of the well leg [2]. A review reported pudendal nerve palsy in 1.9% to 27.6% of patients after orthopaedic procedures using a traction table, mostly transient [8].

lore.intro: Height forum users mention traction and decompression tables alongside hanging and inversion as ways to maximise measured height; the discussion is anecdotal.
